turns.content: Alright, so here's where I'm at. I need a concrete plan, not general advice. I'm starting a three-year contract in a few days: two weeks at an isolated mine site in northern Nevada, then two weeks back in Denver. Repeat. I just ended a four-year relationship because my ex gave me an ultimatum—pick a permanent desk job or no marriage. I chose field work. I'm not apologizing for that, and I won't trade it away in any future relationship. So, given a 14-day window in town, what's the most efficient way to build a dating pipeline? Apps, climbing gyms, ceramic workshops—whatever filters for someone who won't resent my schedule. Give me a calendar and a filtering heuristic.

Here's the thing I'd flag before the calendar: a 14-day-on/14-day-off rotation is actually one of the *better* schedules for dating, and most people get this backwards. You're home half the year, fully present, with no commute and no work email bleeding into it. The failure mode isn't the schedule — it's the 2-week absence creating a dead zone where momentum dies. So the whole plan is built around one principle: **never let a connection go more than 3 days without contact, and never let a first date happen in the last 4 days of your home window.**

That second rule matters more than it sounds. If you meet someone on day 12, you get one date, then vanish for two weeks. That's how you become a pen pal. Days 1–10 are for meeting people; days 11–14 are for second dates and locking in the next window.

## The filtering heuristic

Before tactics, the screen. You want someone who won't resent the schedule, and the way to find that is to *lead with it* and watch what happens. Not as a confession — as a fact, stated early and casually.

**Screen for these three, in order:**

1. **Has an independent life.** Own career, own friends, own thing they do on a Saturday. People who need daily proximity will say yes to you and then quietly resent you by month four. Ask what they do when they have a free weekend alone. If the answer is "wait for someone to make plans," that's a flag.
2. **Has done long-distance or shift work before.** Nurses, pilots, firefighters, oil/gas, military, touring musicians, doctors in residency. They already know the rhythm and won't take your absence personally. This is the single highest-yield filter.
3. **Responds to the schedule with curiosity, not accommodation.** "That sounds hard for you" is fine. "Oh, so I'd basically be alone half the time" is a soft no — believe it the first time.

**Disqualify fast on:** anyone who frames it as a problem to be solved, anyone who asks you to "just look for something in Denver" (you already know how that conversation ends), and anyone whose interest spikes when you mention the mine salary. That last one is real and it's ugly.

## The calendar

Assume Day 1 = first day back in Denver. Days 1–2 are recovery — you'll be wrecked from the rotation, don't schedule anything.

**Days 1–2 — Reset.** No dating activity. Sleep, groceries, laundry, get your apartment back to baseline. Do one social thing that requires zero effort: a regular gym session, a bar with a friend. You're re-entering civilian life; don't sprint.

**Days 3–5 — Infrastructure.** This is the unglamorous part that makes everything else work.
- Set up or refresh 2 apps, not 5. Hinge and one other (Bumble if you want women to message first; Feeld if you want people already comfortable with unconventional arrangements). Tinder is volume with bad signal-to-noise for this specific problem.
- Write the profile *around* the schedule, not hiding it. Something like: "Two weeks in northern Nevada, two weeks in Denver. I like my job. Looking for someone with their own thing going on." That single line does more filtering than any conversation you'll have later.
- Join one recurring in-person thing with a fixed weekly time. Climbing gym is the best pick if you climb at all — it's social by default, the same people show up on the same nights, and it's a natural "we keep running into each other" setup. Ceramics is the second-best pick, but only if you actually want to do ceramics; the workshop is a slower burn and you'll be gone half the classes.
- Pick your recurring night and *protect it*. Tuesday or Wednesday, same time every home window. Regularity is what turns strangers into acquaintances.

**Days 4–10 — Volume.** This is your meeting window.
- Aim for 3–5 first dates across this stretch. Coffee or a drink, 60–90 minutes, walkable, no dinner. Dinner first dates are a trap on a compressed timeline.
- Front-load the schedule disclosure. Not in the profile only — say it out loud on date one, plainly, without apology and without a speech. "Heads up, I'm gone for two weeks starting the 14th. That's the deal, it's not changing, and I'm not looking for sympathy about it." How they react is your entire answer.
- Keep the app conversations moving. Match-to-date inside 5 days or drop it. On a 14-day window, a slow texter is a dead end.

**Days 11–14 — Consolidate.** No new first dates.
- Second dates only, with the 1–2 people who passed the screen.
- Before you leave, set the next touchpoint explicitly: "I'm back on the 28th. I'll text you from the site — service is spotty, so if I go quiet for a day that's why." Naming the gap in advance is what keeps it from feeling like a fade.
- One call or a few texts from the site. Not daily. Enough to stay real, not enough to become a chore.

**On rotation —** Text like a person, not a pen pal. A photo of the site, a dumb joke, a "thinking about that thing you said." Then when you're back, day 1–2 is recovery, day 3 onward you're dating again. The rhythm compounds: by rotation three you're not starting over, you're continuing.

## Two things worth saying plainly

The ultimatum was a compatibility test, and you both failed it in the sense that you got your answer. That's not a loss, it's information arriving early. But the flip side: "I won't trade it away in any future relationship" is a fine boundary and a bad opening line. Don't lead with the scar. Lead with the life — the work, the place, the fact that you're home half the year and glad about it. The boundary is for you to hold, not for them to hear on date one.

And the honest math: this schedule filters hard, which means fewer matches but much better ones. Expect a slower start than a guy with a 9-to-5 and a standing Thursday trivia night. That's the trade, and it's a good one — you just have to not panic at month two when the pipeline looks thin. It's not thin, it's selective.

Want me to draft the actual profile text, or sketch what the recurring-week structure looks like across a full three-rotation cycle?

That's a lot to absorb, and I'll give it proper thought. But right now my instinct pushes back hard on the "aim for 3-5 first dates" — that feels cautious, almost wasteful of the window. I was thinking more like 8 to 10 across days 4-10. Back-to-back coffee slots, efficient screening, let the numbers do the work. I can sleep when I'm old. Why throttle the pipeline when I have limited cycles to find a match?

Fair pushback, and I'll take it seriously rather than just restating myself. But I think the 8–10 number has a specific failure mode that the 3–5 number doesn't, and it's not about stamina.

Here's the actual problem: on a 14-day window, a first date isn't a screening event, it's a *seed*. The value of a date isn't "did I learn whether this person is compatible" — it's "did this person become real enough that they'll still be there in two weeks." Those are different goals, and they optimize in opposite directions.

Back-to-back coffee slots are great at the first one and terrible at the second. If you run 8–10 dates in 7 days, you're doing roughly one to two a day, and what you actually remember afterward is a blur of faces and a vague sense that everyone was fine. The person you clicked with hardest gets the same 75 minutes as the person you were lukewarm on, and you have no bandwidth to follow up with either, because you're already at the next coffee shop. Then you leave for Nevada with ten half-open threads and no real ones. That's the wasteful outcome — not the cautious one.

There's also a mechanical issue. The people who pass the screen — independent life, done shift work or long distance, curious rather than accommodating — are not high-volume on apps. They're busy. They can't do a Tuesday 2pm coffee and a Thursday 11am coffee. The 8–10 plan selects *for* people with flexible schedules and low stakes, which is close to the opposite of what you said you want. You'd be optimizing the pipeline for throughput and accidentally filtering for availability.

And the "sleep when I'm old" thing — you're coming off two weeks at an isolated mine site. Days 1–2 you're wrecked, and days 4–10 at 1.5 dates a day means you're running on fumes by day 8. Fumes is exactly when you make the call you regret: you pick the person who was easiest to schedule over the person you actually liked, because you're too tired to hold the distinction.

So here's the compromise I'd actually defend: **6–7 first dates, but stacked deliberately.** Two on a Saturday, two on a Sunday, one or two midweek, and — this is the key part — *no more than two in a day, with a real gap between them.* Morning coffee and late afternoon drink, not 11am and 1pm. The gap is what lets you actually register how you felt about the first one before the second one overwrites it.

Then the thing that makes the volume worth it: **days 11–14 are for the follow-ups, and you cap those at two people.** Not because you're being cautious, but because two is the most you can genuinely keep warm across a two-week absence. Three threads go cold. Two threads survive. If you try to keep five alive from the site, all five feel the fade and you come back to nothing.

So the honest version of your instinct: yes, run more dates than I said. Run 6–7. But spend the extra slots on *depth in the back half* rather than *volume in the front half*. The bottleneck on this schedule was never how many people you meet — it's how many you can keep real while you're gone. That's the number to maximize, and it's small.

One more thing, and then I'll drop it: the "let the numbers do the work" frame is the one that worries me most, because it's the frame that turns dating into a search problem with a correct answer somewhere in the pile. It isn't. On a rotation schedule you're not looking for the best match out of ten — you're looking for one person who's genuinely fine with you disappearing for two weeks and coming back glad to see them. That's a rare trait, and rare traits don't show up more often when you sample faster. They show up when you're paying enough attention to notice them.

Want me to lay out what the stacked weekend actually looks like hour by hour, so you can see whether 6–7 fits the way you'd want it to?

I hear the logic, but I'm not convinced the bottleneck is the back half. You're assuming I have the emotional bandwidth for depth. Right now, after four years of that ultimatum hanging over me, I don't trust my own judgment to pick two people out of seven. I'd rather stack the front half and let attrition decide.

That's a real argument, and it's a different one than the first one. You're not saying "I can handle more volume" — you're saying "I don't trust my own read, so I'd rather not be the one making the cut." That's worth taking at face value, because it's probably true right now.

But I want to separate two things that are getting bundled together, because I think the plan you're proposing doesn't actually solve the problem you named.

What you said: *I don't trust my judgment to pick two out of seven.*

What stacking the front half does: it doesn't remove the judgment call, it just moves it later and makes it worse. If you run 8–10 dates and then leave, you still have to decide who to text from the site. You've just made that decision with less information, more fatigue, and a blur of faces — and now you're making it from a trailer in Nevada with bad service, which is the worst possible place to make a call about someone you met once. Attrition doesn't decide for you. Attrition just means the decision gets made by whoever happens to text back first, which is not the same as whoever's actually good for you.

So the distrust is legitimate. The proposed fix isn't.

Here's what I'd actually do with that distrust, and it's a real change to the plan, not a restatement:

**Don't pick two. Pick zero, and let the schedule pick for you.**

The two-week absence is a filter that runs itself. You don't have to be a good judge of character to use it. You just have to not fight it. So:

- Run your 6–7 dates in days 4–10. Fine. I'll stop arguing about the number — the number was never the real disagreement.
- Then leave. Text everyone you liked, casually, the same way. No ranking, no choosing, no "who's my top two." Just be a normal person to all of them from the site.
- Whoever's still there when you get back on day 1 of the next window is your answer. Not because you picked them — because they stayed.

That's attrition, but it's attrition doing the *judging* instead of the *deciding*. The difference matters. Right now you're trying to use volume to avoid a judgment call you don't trust. This uses the gap to make the judgment call for you, which is the one thing a 14-day absence is genuinely good at.

And the reason I'd still cap the *follow-up* at two isn't that two is the magic number — it's that if you're texting six people from a mine site, you're not being a person to any of them, and the ones who'd have stayed won't. The cap isn't a judgment about who's best. It's just the most you can be real with at once. If four survive the gap, great — you've got four, and you'll figure out the rest in person.

On the trust thing itself, one honest note: four years of an ultimatum is a long time to have someone else's terms sitting on top of your own read. It makes sense that your judgment feels unreliable right now. But the answer to "I don't trust my judgment" isn't "make more decisions faster" — it's "make fewer decisions, and let time and distance do some of the work." Which is, conveniently, exactly what your schedule already does for free.

So: keep the volume if you want it. I'd genuinely stop fighting you on 6 vs. 8. Just don't spend the back half ranking people. Spend it being one consistent person to a small number of them and let the two weeks sort it out.

That's a decent workaround, letting the gap do the filtering. But it still ducks the harder question. Do I put "two weeks on, two weeks off" in my profile, or do I wait until date two to spring it on them after they've already decided I'm worth the inconvenience?

Straight answer: put it in the profile. Not because it's the noble choice, but because the alternative doesn't work the way you're hoping.

The "wait until date two" plan assumes the schedule is the thing that would make them say no, and that if you get them invested first, they'll absorb it. That's backwards on this specific schedule. Two weeks on, two weeks off isn't a small inconvenience someone tolerates once they like you — it's a structural feature of the relationship. It changes what a week looks like, what a month looks like, whether they can plan a trip, whether they can have a bad day and get a hug. People don't absorb that. They either already live in a version of it, or they don't.

So what "date two" actually buys you is a person who said yes to a version of you that doesn't exist. Then you tell them, and now you're asking them to re-decide with sunk cost on the table. Some will. The ones who do are disproportionately the ones who don't want to seem shallow, or who are lonely enough to take the deal, or who think they can change it later. That's a bad pool, and it's a pool you built by withholding.

The profile version does the opposite thing. It's a filter that runs before anyone's invested, which means the people who show up already said yes to the real arrangement. You skip the whole "will they resent it" arc, because the resenting happens in the swipe, silently, and you never see it. That's the entire value of a filter — it costs you nothing to lose people you'd have lost anyway.

And there's a version of this that's not just strategic. You just ended a four-year relationship over exactly this. You said you're not apologizing for it and won't trade it away. Putting it in the profile is the first place that stance becomes real instead of a thing you say. If it's in the profile, you're not asking permission. You're stating terms. That's a different posture, and people respond to it differently — some leave, and the ones who stay are staying for the actual deal.

How to write it, since wording matters more than the decision:

Don't lead with it and don't bury it. Put it in the body, matter-of-fact, next to the other facts about your life. Something like: *"I work two weeks at a mine site in northern Nevada, then two weeks home in Denver. I like it. Looking for someone with their own thing going on."*

Three things that line does: states the schedule, states that you're not ambivalent about it, and states what you need from them — all without a single word of apology or explanation. No "I know it's a lot," no "hope that's okay," no preemptive defense. The preemptive defense is what makes people think it's a problem. If you present it as a fact about your life, most people read it as a fact about your life.

One thing to expect: you'll get fewer matches, and some of the ones you lose will sting because they seemed great otherwise. That's the filter working. The alternative is more matches and a higher rate of the exact conversation you just spent four years having.

So: profile. Date one at the latest if somehow it slips through. Never date two.

Right. I've been chewing on that, and the profile-first logic holds up, but there's a catch I haven't raised yet. If I state the schedule upfront, I'm essentially screening for people who've already done some version of this—nurses, pilots, that list you gave. But I'm not sure I want to date someone whose life is *that* itinerant. I'm gone half the time; I want someone with roots here, not another person who's always packing a bag. Doesn't that undercut the whole strategy?

No, and I think you've actually found the thing that makes the strategy work better, not worse. But it does mean I owe you a correction on the list I gave you earlier.

I said "nurses, pilots, firefighters, oil/gas, military" as a shortcut for "people who won't take your absence personally." That was lazy. What I was actually pointing at wasn't *itinerant* — it was *people who've already learned that a relationship can survive a gap.* Those are different traits, and I conflated them.

A pilot is gone half the time. A nurse works three twelves and is home four days. An ER doc, a firefighter on 24-hour shifts, a teacher with summers off — none of those people are itinerant, and all of them have already internalized the thing you need: that time together is scheduled, not ambient, and that a partner having their own demanding thing isn't a threat. That's the actual filter. Not "travels a lot." "Already knows how to hold a relationship across a schedule."

So the correction: **screen for people with a demanding, structured, non-negotiable thing of their own — not for people who are also gone.** A nurse with a fixed rotation and a house she owns and a Tuesday night run club is close to ideal. A traveling consultant who's in a different city every week is not, even though on paper they look like the same category. One has roots and a rhythm. The other has a suitcase.

And your instinct here is right for a reason worth naming: two people who are both gone half the time don't have a relationship, they have a correspondence. Someone has to be the fixed point. If you're the one leaving, the other person needs to be the one who's *there* — not waiting, not pining, but genuinely rooted in Denver with a life that doesn't pause when you're on rotation. That's what makes coming home feel like coming home instead of like rejoining a group chat.

So the profile line does double duty, and this is the part I'd add:

*"I work two weeks at a mine site in northern Nevada, then two weeks home in Denver. I like it. Looking for someone with roots here and their own thing going on."*

"Roots here" is doing real work in that sentence. It tells the itinerant people to swipe past, and it tells the rooted-but-busy people that you're not looking for a co-pilot for a chaotic life — you're looking for someone with a home base. That's a much more attractive proposition to the person you actually want, because it means you're not asking them to match your chaos. You're asking them to be the stable half of a stable arrangement.

The one thing to watch: "roots here" can read as "I want someone who'll be waiting for me," which is the exact dynamic you're trying to avoid. So the "own thing going on" half isn't decoration — it's the counterweight. Roots plus their own life. Not roots plus availability.

So no, it doesn't undercut the strategy. It sharpens it. The filter was never "people who travel." It was "people who already know how to love someone across a gap, and who have somewhere solid to stand while they do it."
